title: Effective context engineering for AI agents
author: Anthropic
takes: Context rot and an attention budget: more tokens, worse recall. Three tools for long work - compaction (risks losing what matters later), structured notes outside the window (NOTES.md), sub-agents that return 1-2 thousand token summaries; load knowledge just in time by reference.

title: Effective harnesses for long-running agents
author: Anthropic
takes: Compaction alone was not enough: each fresh session gets up to speed from a progress file, the git log and a feature list, works one item, commits and writes its progress. Whether specialised agents beat one general agent is left open.

title: Orchestrate teams of Claude Code sessions
author: Anthropic
takes: Teammates message each other directly, not only through the lead; 3-5 teammates; each starts from project context and a spawn prompt, never the lead's history; in-process teammates are not restored on resume; for routine or sequential work one session is cheaper.

title: Claude Code agent memory frontmatter
author: shanraisshan
takes: Since v2.1.33 a subagent can keep its own MEMORY.md (project scope in .claude/agent-memory/NAME/), its first 200 lines put in its prompt each time: the field writes expertise down per role rather than keeping it in a session; each role's memory is siloed from the others.

title: Multi-Agents: What's Actually Working
author: Walden Yan (Cognition)
takes: A narrower class works: writes stay single-threaded and extra agents contribute intelligence, not actions. Consulting a 'smart friend' works best by sharing a fork of the asker's full context; unstructured swarms of negotiating agents are a distraction.

title: Benchmarking Multi-Agent Architectures
author: Will Fu-Hinthorn (LangChain)
takes: A supervisor that relays every message plays telephone: it scored lower and spent more tokens than agents handing off directly; removing routing chatter from the workers' context closed much of the gap.

title: Agentic Context Engineering: Evolving Contexts for Self-Improving Language Models
author: Zhang et al.
takes: Knowledge kept by rewriting one summary erodes (context collapse) and drifts toward the terse (brevity bias); itemised, incremental additions to a playbook keep the detail. ICLR 2026.

title: Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?
author: Cemri et al.
takes: 1600+ traces, 14 failure modes in three groups: system design, misalignment between agents (lost context, ignored input, withheld information), task verification. Gains from multi-agent systems are often minimal. NeurIPS 2025.

title: Context Rot: How Increasing Input Tokens Impacts LLM Performance
author: Hong, Troynikov, Huber (Chroma)
takes: Models do worse as input grows, even on simple tasks and well below the window's size; focused inputs beat full ones.

title: Exploring Advanced LLM Multi-Agent Systems Based on Blackboard Architecture
author: Han and Zhang
takes: Agents share one blackboard instead of private memories; a control unit picks who acts from what is on it. With 2510.01285 (agents volunteer for requests posted to the board): routing by a shared record, not by a central relay.

title: Sleep-time Compute
author: Letta
takes: Stateful agents keep editable memory blocks; a separate agent rewrites them between tasks into clean, concise learned context, so the working agent need not re-derive it.
